papers.title: A Qualitative Study Investigating Sex Differences in the Needs and Priorities of Lower Limb Prosthesis Users
papers.abstract: BackgroundQualitative methods can facilitate understanding of the unique experiences of female lower limb prosthesis users (LLPUs) and inform sex-specific rehabilitation and prosthetic design. Given their underrepresentation in research, meaningful collaboration with female LLPUs is imperative to ensure efforts reflect their priorities. ObjectiveCollaborate with female LLPUs to develop an interview guide with female-specific priorities and use it to investigate potential sex differences in needs of LLPUs. Study DesignQualitative research study. MethodsFive female LLPUs were engaged to develop an interview guide, targeting aspects of a users prosthesis, and physical and psychosocial aspects of daily life. LLPUs were interviewed online and data were analyzed collaboratively using Codebook Thematic Analysis. Themes were extracted and assessed for sex differences. ResultsInterviews were conducted with 18 LLPUs (9-female, 9-male). Themes arose in four categories: 1-Prosthetic, 2-Physical, 3-Psychosocial, and 4-Financial Experiences, with sex differences observed in all but the financial category. Prosthetic themes revealed female-specific challenges with prosthetic fit, motivating future research into sex-specific prostheses. Physical themes expand understanding of female-specific ambulation challenges, presenting implications for sex-specific rehabilitation. Finally, psychosocial themes present new insight into sex-specific psychosocial experiences, including frustrations with clinicians and concerns regarding maternity and child-rearing. ConclusionExtracted themes demonstrated an array of sex-specific experiences, which can inform future research to address sex-specific rehabilitation and prosthetic design. Clinical RelevanceThis study identified sex-specific prosthetic, physical, and psychosocial challenges experienced by female LLPUs, underscoring the need for more sex-specific rehabilitation and prosthetic care. These findings can inform patient-centered clinical practice and guide future development of sex-specific prosthetic design and rehabilitation strategies.

papers.title: Effects of an exercise prescription system (ACTIVE) on physical function in community-dwelling older adults: protocol for a single-centre, assessor-blinded, parallel-group randomised controlled trial
papers.abstract: BackgroundAs Chinas population continues to age, preserving physical function in older adults is an important goal of healthy ageing. Digital health interventions have been used to promote physical activity. Comparative evaluation of specific programmes is needed to determine whether individualised exercise prescriptions informed by multidimensional functional assessment provide additional functional benefits. MethodsThis single-centre, assessor-blinded, parallel-group randomised controlled trial planned sample size of 142 community-dwelling adults aged 60-85 years in Beijing. Participants will be allocated 1:1 to the ACTIVE group or the standardised, non-individualised exercise group (71 per group) for an 8-week intervention. The primary outcome is the physical function composite Z-score at week 8. It is the unweighted mean of four measures after aligning their directions and standardising them against baseline values: 4-m gait speed, five-times sit-to-stand time, 6-min walk distance and eyes-open single-leg stance time. Secondary outcomes include the raw values and Z-scores of the four components, physical activity measured with the International Physical Activity Questionnaire Short Form (IPAQ-SF), health-related quality of life measured with the EQ-5D-5L, chair sit-and-reach performance, lower-limb muscle strength and the strength asymmetry index, and handgrip strength. DiscussionThis trial will evaluate the short-term effects of ACTIVE on physical function in community-dwelling older adults, providing preliminary clinical evidence for assessment-informed individualised home-based exercise and informing subsequent research and community implementation. Trial registrationChinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2600117481). Registered on 26 January 2026. https://www.chictr.org.cn/

papers.title: Defining Constructs of Hand Function Quality at Home After Cervical Spinal Cord Injury Through Egocentric Videos: A Qualitative Inquiry
papers.abstract: IntroductionLoss of hand function is an impactful consequence of cervical spinal cord injury (cSCI), affecting activities of daily living (ADLs). Hand function assessments play an important role in developing interventions that mitigate these impacts. However, assessment can be complicated by factors including the diversity of grasps and use of assistive devices. Consequently, standardized assessments in clinical environments do not fully reflect function in real-world settings. This gap has resulted in increasing interest in assessing hand function at home through wearable cameras (egocentric video) to provide information about real-world hand use. Despite advancements, a framework is required to describe the quality of hand use when observing unconstrained tasks through egocentric video. This study aimed to define constructs that describe hand function quality in unconstrained, in-home activities after cSCI, captured through egocentric videos. MethodsA qualitative study was conducted using focus groups (N=17) to generate a list of constructs defining good quality hand use in unconstrained environments after cSCI through egocentric videos. Individuals with cSCI, physicians, therapists, and researchers participated. Content analysis was used to identify patterns, codes and categories. ResultsFourteen categories and thirty-three constructs were identified. While several constructs were common across groups, distinct perspectives also emerged highlighting the multidimensional nature of hand function. DiscussionPerceptions of meaningful hand function encompass a broad range of constructs, emphasizing the importance of both functional performance and motor control aspects. The identified constructs provide a basis for the development of novel metrics of hand function in the context of real-world ADLs.

papers.title: Older Adults and Healthcare Professionals Perspectives on Comfort, Dignity, and Safety During Technology-Assisted Transfers: A Qualitative Descriptive Study
papers.abstract: PurposeThe experience of comfort, dignity, and safety during the use of transfer technologies remains poorly understood despite evidence supporting their effectiveness in reducing work-related musculoskeletal injuries among healthcare professionals. This study explored how older adults and healthcare professionals understand and experience comfort, dignity, and safety during technology-assisted transfers. Materials and MethodsA qualitative descriptive study guided by reflexive thematic analysis was conducted across three healthcare facilities in Ottawa, Canada. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 15 older adults and long-term care residents requiring technology-assisted transfers, and four focus group discussions were conducted with 15 healthcare professionals. Data were analyzed using Braun and Clarkes reflexive thematic analysis. ResultsFindings revealed an overarching theme: the relational nature of the transfer experience. Comfort, dignity, and safety were experienced as interconnected and reciprocal rather than as distinct outcomes. Three dimensions were identified: (1) comfort, which was physical, emotional, and relational; (2) dignity, which was restored through how staff treated the person; and (3) safety, which depended on trust in the person operating the device and, for professionals, on clinical judgment and adaptability. Participants also highlighted the importance of staff training, equipment customization, communication, and adequate staffing to enhance transfer experiences. ConclusionComfort, dignity, and safety during technology-assisted transfers are not inherent properties of transfer devices but are co-constructed through interactions among older adults, healthcare professionals, and technologies. Transfer quality depended on relational practices, such as communication, privacy, and staff continuity, alongside technical competence. Training that combines technical and relational skills, stable staffing, and adaptable equipment may improve transfer experiences.

papers.title: Thoracic expansion and spirometry 120 days after adding diaphragmatic manual therapy to physiotherapy in non-specific low back pain: Follow-up of a randomized controlled trial
papers.abstract: ObjectiveAn interim analysis of the DIAFRAGMA trial (46 participants) found that adding manual diaphragmatic stretching to physiotherapy improved thoracic expansion, forced vital capacity and forced expiratory volume in one second up to 30 days in non-specific low back pain. We assessed whether these differences persist at 120 days and, exploratorily, whether baseline values moderate the response. MethodsIn this parallel-group, assessor-blinded randomized controlled trial, 55 adults were randomized and 50 were analysed (22 experimental, 28 control). All participants received ten sessions of conventional physiotherapy; the experimental group also received manual diaphragmatic stretching in six of them. Thoracic expansion (cirtometry at three levels) and portable spirometry were assessed at baseline, after the first and tenth sessions, and 7, 30 and 120 days after treatment. Between-group differences were estimated with linear mixed-effects models and false discovery rate correction. ResultsAt 120 days, inspiratory thoracic expansion was greater in the experimental group at the axillary (3.38 cm; 95% CI 2.94 to 3.81), xiphoid (3.52 cm; 2.78 to 4.26) and basal levels (4.12 cm; 3.36 to 4.88). Forced vital capacity (1.57 L; 0.96 to 2.18), forced expiratory volume in one second (1.49 L; 0.97 to 2.01) and peak expiratory flow (2.70 L/s; 1.21 to 4.19) were also higher (all p < 0.001). These differences arose during treatment and remained stable thereafter. Expiratory-phase expansion and mid-to-late expiratory flows did not improve. No baseline value moderated the response. ConclusionsAdding manual diaphragmatic stretching to physiotherapy was associated with greater inspiratory chest expansion and higher spirometric values that were maintained at 120 days. Because of the size of the spirometric differences, the portable spirometry protocol and the lack of participant blinding and a sham comparator, these findings require confirmation in sham-controlled trials using laboratory spirometry. Trial registrationClinicalTrials.gov NCT06069388.

papers.title: Multimodal Prehabilitation in People Awaiting Acute Inpatient Cardiac Surgery (PreP-ACe): A single-arm feasibility study
papers.abstract: IntroductionThe average waiting time for urgent coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) is 13 days in England and Wales and 27 days in Northern Ireland; significantly longer than the National Institute for Cardiovascular Outcomes Research (NICOR) recommendation of 7 days. Inpatients are at risk of Hospital-Associated Deconditioning (HAD) which impacts cognitive and physical function, increases mortality and healthcare cost. Prehabilitation has been shown to improve physical function and reduce complications in the elective population. Prehabilitation has never been attempted in acute inpatients waiting for cardiac surgery. MethodsParticipants were recruited between April 2024 and February 2025. Once consented, the participants were provided with psychoeducation booklet and underwent assessments; 6 minute walk test (6MWT), hand grip test (HGT), spirometry, EQ-5D-5L and cardiac anxiety questionnaire (CAQ) on day 0, 7 and 14. The physiotherapy team assessed and prescribed personalised exercise. Information regarding their in-hospital stay were collected. Our primary outcome was determining the feasibility of prehabilitation. The secondary outcome was to identify any adverse events related to the intervention and changes in the assessment results. Results17 participants were recruited resulting in a recruitment rate of 1.5 participants per month. 1 participant withdrew from the study. 7 participants were seen by physiotherapist and participated in the exercise program. The adherence to the exercise program was 100% with tolerability of >80%. No adverse events related to exercise recorded. 11 participants remained in the study for 7 days or more. DiscussionPrehabilitation is a novel concept of preparing inpatients for acute cardiac surgery. There are several challenges in determining the feasibility of prehabilitation in this population. These include identifying the best time to recruit, optimal level of exercise, funding (staffing to execute the intervention) and clinician reception towards the intervention. However, prehabilitation was well accepted, tolerated and adhered to by participants.

papers.title: Previewing gaze behaviours predict gait speed, risky stepping strategies and cognitive dual task cost in older adults
papers.abstract: BackgroundPrevious work demonstrated that route previewing improves adaptive gait performance in older adults. However, it is unknown if specific gaze behaviours during previewing are associated with these benefits. Specifically, little is known about how older adults visually scan future walking routes during a given previewing period and whether different gaze behaviours are associated with subsequent walking performance. MethodsGaze and gait data were collected from 29 older adults (Mage = 73.9, SD = 8.1 years; n = 19 female) during dual-task adaptive walking, preceded by a 10-second period in which they were instructed to preview their walking route. Eye-tracking measures across defined areas of interest during previewing and subsequent gait measures were analysed using linear and generalized mixed-effects models to determine whether previewing gaze behaviours predicted gait outcomes and cognitive dual-task cost. ResultsGreater gaze sequence complexity (LZC_task) during previewing was associated with lower cognitive dual-task cost during walking, Larger gaze transition sizes predicted slower walking speed while greater duration of distal fixation allocation was associated with an increased likelihood of risky stepping behaviours. No previewing gaze behaviours predicted more than one gait outcome, and no significant relationships were observed between gaze behaviours and stepping errors. ConclusionsDifferent aspects of visual previewing were associated with distinct locomotor and cognitive outcomes. Greater gaze-sequence complexity was associated with lower cognitive dual-task cost. In contrast, larger gaze transitions predicted slower walking. Together, these findings suggest that effective previewing may depend on integrating proximal and distal route information into a coherent prospective stepping plan, rather than simply looking further ahead. Understanding how older adults visually plan upcoming routes may help inform approaches to reducing dual-task-related impairments in adaptive walking.

papers.title: Physical calibration and signal periodic updates to synchronize IMUs for 5-day continuous knee flexion tracking
papers.abstract: Wearable inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors provide a promising method to assess real-world human motion kinematics. However, multi-day multi-IMU tracking is difficult due to the desynchronization driven by inaccurate IMU clocks. In this study, 15 volunteers wore IMUs continuously on their thighs and shanks for 5 weekdays (Mon-Fri), which included 3 repeated in-lab motion capture sessions. We synchronized thigh and shank IMUs using two methods. The first was physical calibration, where we maneuvered the IMUs in a rigid holder to produce sync signals pre-donning (Mon) and post-doffing (Fri), then linearly resampled data from one IMU to match the other via cross-correlation. The second was signal-based periodic updates, where we shifted IMU clocks hourly based on the timewise alignment of preprocessed body-worn acceleration signals. After syncing, we used sensor-to-segment alignment and accelerometer-gyroscope fusion to estimate knee flexion and compared results to camera-based motion capture. Physical calibration alone removed clock offset in most cases, where IMU-estimated knee flexion generally matched motion capture (correlation [≥]0.944; root-mean-square difference RMSD [≤]6.9{degrees}). But in some participants, residual mid-week desynchronization ([~]0.2s) resulted in misestimated knee flexion (Wed: RMSD up to [~]19{degrees}). After applying signal-based updates or combining it with physical calibration, IMU matched motion capture on all 3 days (Mon: r [≥]0.975, RMSD [≤]6.1{degrees}; Wed: r [≥]0.971, RMSD [≤]6.2{degrees}, Fri: r [≥]0.977; RMSD [≤]5.9{degrees}). Our multi-modal synchronization enables week-long knee flexion tracking and lays a foundation for advanced syncing tools, for improving the feasibility of wearable multi-IMU systems to continuously monitor real-world knee kinematics in clinical studies.

papers.title: From "Tech Fear" to Digital Self-Efficacy: A COM-B and TDF Analysis of Tele-Exercise Engagement in Older Adults at Risk of Falls
papers.abstract: BackgroundTele-exercise offers an alternative approach to physical activity for older adults, however remote delivery introduces distinctive challenges. ObjectivesNested within a 3-month randomised controlled trial (RCT), this qualitative study explored the experiences of community-dwelling older adults at risk of falls who completed synchronous tele-exercise, mapping findings to the COM-B model, Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF), and Behaviour Change Techniques (BCTs) to inform intervention design. MethodsSemi-structured interviews and delivery format preference queries were conducted with 25 purposively sampled older adults following the intervention. Data were analysed using hybrid thematic analysis integrated with COM-B, TDF, and the Behaviour Change Wheel (BCW). ResultsDespite baseline digital literacy barriers, participants engaged successfully across six themes: Technological Skills, Access & Support; Coach Support & Exercise Adaptability; Health Motivation & Goal Achievement; Emotional Journey with Technology; Home Environment & Accessibility; and Social Interaction Dynamics. Core BCTs addressing low digital literacy and physical limitations included practical social support (in-home onboarding), environmental restructuring (hardware setup), graded tasks, and social reward. These techniques facilitated an emotional transition from initial apprehension to pride, fostering digital self-efficacy. Notably, an implementation paradox emerged: while over half preferred face-to-face (f2f) delivery, they demonstrated high adherence in tele -exercise programme, indicating that delivery preference does not preclude digital capability. ConclusionTele-exercise is feasible and acceptable for older adults at risk of falls, challenging assumptions that low digital literacy precludes digital health adoption. Embedding targeted BCTs within a scaffolded framework addresses structural and psychological barriers, reinforcing digital self-efficacy to sustain remote participation. Key PointsO_LITele-exercise is feasible when behaviour techniques shift participants from digital anxiety to self-efficacy. C_LIO_LIRemote delivery removes transport barriers but requires personalized home-safety checks to address domestic hazards. C_LIO_LISocial connectedness, peer modelling, and instructor feedback transform isolated routines into engaging communal experiences. C_LIO_LIClinicians should prescribe structured tele-exercise with standardized onboarding and targeted techniques to reduce fall risks. papers.title: CHANGES IN CERVICAL MUSCLE MECHANICAL PROPERTIES DURING OROFACIAL MOTOR TASKS IN INDIVIDUALS WITH AND WITHOUT CHRONIC NECK PAIN
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo investigate changes in cervical muscle mechanical properties during tongue-pressure tasks and maximum intercuspation (MIC) in individuals with chronic neck pain and healthy controls, and to explore associations between these properties, cervical mobility, tongue pressure, pain intensity, and neck disability. MethodsEighty-four adults participated, including 42 individuals with chronic neck pain and 42 healthy controls. Myotonometry assessed frequency, stiffness, logarithmic decrement, relaxation time, and creep in the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) and trapezius muscles during tongue-pressure tasks at 50%, 80%, and 100% of maximum tongue pressure (MTP) and during maximum intercuspation. Group-by-condition effects were examined using linear mixed-effects models. Exploratory correlations and cervical mobility assessments were conducted in a subsample of 36 participants. ResultsTongue-pressure conditions showed significant effects on cervical muscle mechanical properties in 19 of 20 mixed-effects models at the nominal significance level, particularly for frequency, stiffness, relaxation time, and creep. Maximum intercuspation was associated with changes in frequency and stiffness in both muscles, with additional changes in relaxation time and creep in the sternocleidomastoid. Group-by-condition interactions were generally nonsignificant, apart from an isolated interaction involving right trapezius logarithmic decrement. The neck pain group exhibited lower absolute tongue-pressure values at 80% and 100% of maximum tongue pressure. Exploratory analyses identified reduced cervical extension and rotation, together with associations between cervical mobility, myotonometric properties, pain intensity, and tongue pressure. ConclusionsOrofacial motor tasks were associated with changes in cervical muscle mechanical properties regardless of chronic neck pain status. Although clinical characteristics were associated with selected mechanical and functional measures, chronic neck pain did not consistently modify task-related cervical responses. These findings support functional interactions between cervical and orofacial systems.

papers.title: Wearable Sensors Predict Exertion Without Changes in Pulse Rate for Frail End-Stage Kidney Disease Patients
papers.abstract: End-Stage Kidney Disease (ESKD) patients require careful exertion monitoring during prehabilitation to ensure safety and efficacy. Traditional prehabilitation typically relies on heart rate to estimate physical exertion; however, this is problematic for ESKD patients due to their lower physical capacity and the high prevalence of beta-blocker prescriptions, which prevent typical heart rate responses during exercise. In this study, we investigated whether multi-modal wearable sensors could better predict the Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) in (N=13) ESKD patients and (N=13) healthy older adult controls. We collected continuous physiological data--including pulse rate, electrodermal activity, skin temperature, and accelerometer data--using a commercial smartwatch during prehabilitation sessions. Using individualized machine learning pipelines, we compared regression models built solely on pulse rate against comprehensive multi-feature models. We found distinct differences between the groups: baseline pulse-rate models performed substantially worse for the ESKD cohort, whereas they maintained predictive validity for controls. Conversely, multi-feature models significantly improved predictive performance for ESKD participants, achieving a Root Mean Square Error of 1.33. Feature selection confirmed that ESKD models relied heavily on physiological data beyond pulse rate to compensate for the lack of cardiovascular variability. These results demonstrate that heart rate alone is an insufficient biomarker for this population, and that remote exertion monitoring for ESKD patients requires distinct, multi-modal predictive algorithms rather than those designed for healthy adults.

papers.title: Physical and psychosocial outcomes in children with limb loss 2-years after the 2023 Kahramanmaras-Türkiye earthquakes
papers.abstract: IntroductionThe 2023 Kahramanmaras-Turkiye earthquakes resulted in many paediatric amputations. While prosthetic provision following disasters has been described, little is known about longer-term physical and psychosocial outcomes in children with earthquake-related limb loss. AimEvaluate health-related quality of life, prosthesis experience, pain, and function approximately two years post-amputation. MethodRetrospective analysis was conducted of children with earthquake-related limb loss who attend the XXX Center. Socio-demographic and amputation-related data, psychological status, outcome scores for pain, the Paediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) and the Trinity Amputation and Prosthesis Experience Scales (TAPES) were included. ResultsFifty-six children (50% female; 13.7{+/-}5.0 years old) were included. Children had unilateral upper limb loss (n=15), unilateral lower limb loss (n=31), bilateral lower limb loss (n=7), or combined upper and lower limb loss (n=3). Data were obtained 2.3{+/-}0.4 years following amputation. Median child-reported PedsQL scores were 72.3/100.0, with high social functioning (85.0/100.0) but lower emotional functioning (60.0/100.0). No differences in PedsQL outcomes were found between limb loss groups. Children rated their physical and emotional quality of life higher than carers rated them. TAPES median scores were 50.0/75.0 for psychosocial adjustment, 16.0/36.0 for activity restriction, and 34.5/45.0 for prosthetic satisfaction. Children with unilateral lower limb loss demonstrated superior adjustment and prosthetic satisfaction than children with unilateral upper limb or bilateral lower limb loss (p<0.05). ConclusionsChildren demonstrated favourable physical, social, and school-related quality of life 2.3 years after the earthquakes. However, emotional wellbeing remained affected, highlighting the importance of long-term mental health support alongside prosthetic and rehabilitation services.

papers.title: Individualized systems-informed corrective exercise for adults meeting prespecified criteria for upper crossed syndrome: protocol for a randomized controlled trial
papers.abstract: BackgroundHeterogeneity in eligibility criteria, intervention content, and exercise-progression rules has limited the reproducibility of research on upper crossed syndrome. This trial will examine the added effect of a structured, individualized, staged corrective-exercise program on adults who meet prespecified criteria for this phenotype. MethodsIn this parallel randomized controlled trial, 36 women and men aged 18-40 years with forward head and shoulder posture and increased thoracic kyphosis will be allocated 1:1, stratified by sex. Over 12 weeks, both groups will attend three sessions per week and receive stationary cycling, indication-based stretching and mobilization, and education on healthy movement habits. The intervention group will additionally receive a systems-informed program encompassing restoration of range of motion, muscle-activation retraining, correction of movement patterns, progressive load tolerance, and preparation for health-enhancing physical activity. The primary outcome is the baseline-adjusted week-12 between-group difference in a multivariate profile comprising the forward-head, forward-shoulder, and thoracic-kyphosis angles. Scapular-muscle electromyography, range of motion, and balance are secondary outcomes. The primary exploratory electroencephalographic outcome is change in central relative alpha power during quiet standing with eyes open. Posture, range of motion, and balance will be assessed at baseline, week 12, and four-week follow-up; electromyography and electroencephalography at baseline and week 12. The primary analysis will use MANCOVA adjusted for baseline and sex, with Pillais trace; longitudinal analyses will use linear mixed models. Effect estimates and 95% confidence intervals will be reported. ConclusionsThis study will test the added effect of a reproducible corrective-exercise framework beyond the shared active-control components. The four-week follow-up will not support inference about long-term prevention of recurrence. Ethics and trial registrationEthics approval: IR.UI.REC.1404.053. Trial registration: IRCT20250921067305N1.

papers.title: User Experience of a Rehab Community-Based, Affordable Robot Exercise System (Rehab CARES) for Gamified Motor and Cognitive Stroke Rehabilitation
papers.abstract: PurposeRobot-assisted therapy predominantly targets motor impairment, although post-stroke motor and cognitive impairments co-occur. We report user experience in a longitudinal deployment of a Rehab Community-based Affordable Robot Exercise System (RehabCARES) for delivering personalized motor/cognitive training. MethodsSix adults with chronic stroke (FM-UE 20-61; MoCA 22-28) completed 12 therapy visits with THEAbot, a reconfigurable 1-DoF robot. Rehab CARES also included a haptic/biometric dynamic difficulty adjustment controller and eight games characterized by cognitive processes and motor/cognitive demand. We report gaming preference, usage, and user experience (pain, exertion, usability, affect, workload) across therapy. ResultsUser experience varied, but generally, self-reported pain was low, perceived exertion was light to moderate, enjoyment was strong and stable, and sense of control increased while excitement plateaued. Workload showed decreasing frustration and effort. Game selection during therapy was partially consistent with motor/cognitive clinical profiles; preferences and perceptual abilities may have influenced choices. Usability scores exceeded acceptability at all time points, peaking at the final visit (86 {+/-} 4.5 out of 100). ConclusionsRehabCARES provided personalized motor/cognitive training to a heterogeneous cohort in a community-based setting, delivering a positive user experience. Hardware reconfigurability and motor/cognitive game variety likely enabled this success. Trial registrationClinicalTrials.gov, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05542121, NCT05542121.

papers.title: Early Prediction of Discharge Outcomes in Geriatric Rehabilitation: Development and Temporal Validation of a Multiclass Model
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo develop and validate a model that predicts on day 7 of subacute rehabilitation (timed to inform the first multidisciplinary team meeting) the probabilities of three mutually exclusive outcomes: minimal dependency, nursing-care dependency, or medical deterioration. DesignRetrospective cohort study with temporal validation. Multinomial regression and XGBoost models were trained on 80% of admissions during the years 2016-2024 of members of the largest national health maintenance organization (HMO), tested on the remaining 20% and members of other HMOs, and validated on year 2025 admissions. Models output patient-level outcome probabilities with the strongest feature contributors. SettingA public geriatric rehabilitation hospital. ParticipantsAll consecutive first admissions (N=10,920; median age 80 years; median length of stay 35 days). InterventionsNot applicable. Main Outcome MeasuresDischarge disposition: minimal dependency, nursing-care dependency, or medical deterioration (transfer to acute care without return, or in-hospital death). Predictors were demographic, functional, cognitive, clinical, and laboratory variables documented before day 7 with linkage to pre-admission community health records. Performance was assessed by multiclass area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), Brier score and positive predictive value (PPV). ResultsOverall, 34% of patients were discharged with minimal dependency, 44% with nursing-care dependency, and 22% deteriorated medically. Both models performed comparably. Multinomial regression achieved an AUC of 0.81 (95% CI: 0.79-0.83) compared with 0.72 (0.71-0.73) for FIM alone, and it was maintained on temporal validation (AUC 0.80, 0.78-0.82). At a [≥]60% probability threshold, the model flagged 32% of patients for nursing-care dependency and 5% for deterioration, with PPVs of 72% and 69%, respectively. ConclusionsDay-7 multiclass risk estimation from routinely collected data is feasible, interpretable and stable over time. Alerts could prompt earlier social-work involvement and closer monitoring of patients at risk of deterioration; prospective controlled evaluation is warranted.

papers.title: Five Days of Acute Intermittent Hypoxia Is Safe and Improves Somatic Motor Function in Persons with Multiple Sclerosis
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVESWalking impairment affects up to 75% of persons with multiple sclerosis (MS), and the benefits of rehabilitation are constrained by limited capacity for training-induced neuroplasticity. Acute intermittent hypoxia (AIH), brief repeated exposures to low inspired oxygen, triggers serotonin-dependent spinal plasticity that enhances motor output. In spinal cord injury, daily AIH paired with walking training has produced larger walking gains than training alone, positioning AIH as a promising primer for rehabilitation. Before AIH can be combined with training in MS, its safety and stand-alone effects with repeated daily dosing must be established in a population with demyelinating disease. We therefore conducted the first multi-day AIH trial in persons with MS to characterize safety and tolerability and to evaluate preliminary effects on ankle strength and walking. METHODSTwenty-three ambulatory adults with MS (Expanded Disability Status Scale [EDSS] 3.0-6.5; 15 relapsing-remitting, 8 secondary-progressive) completed a randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Participants received AIH (15 x [~]60 s episodes; FiO{square} =0.09; SpO{square} target 84-88%) and Sham in a counterbalanced order, separated by a [≥]4-week washout. Assessments at pre-intervention, post-intervention, and follow-up included ankle plantarflexion and dorsiflexion torque, 6-Minute Walk Test (6MWT), Timed 25-Foot Walk (T25FW), and MS Walking Scale-12 (MSWS-12). Treatment effects were estimated using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) with participant as a random effect. RESULTSNo serious adverse events related to the intervention were reported, and follow-up MRI showed no new MS activity in either arm. Mean nadir SpO{square} during AIH was 84.7 {+/-} 0.2%, and cardiovascular parameters returned to baseline within minutes of each session completion. Ankle plantarflexion torque was significantly greater following AIH than Sham ({beta}= 8.74 N{middle dot}m, p < 0.001), with mean increases of 17.5% at post-intervention and 29.2% at follow-up. Six-minute walk distance was also significantly greater after AIH ({beta}= 10.14 m, p = 0.039). Dorsiflexion torque (p = 0.202), T25FW time (p = 0.239), and MSWS-12 score (p = 0.564) did not differ significantly between conditions. Greater elevation in heart rate during hypoxic episodes was associated with larger strength gains at follow-up (r = 0.58, p = 0.009). CONCLUSIONSDaily AIH sessions are safe and well tolerated in persons with MS across a clinically heterogeneous disability range and produce significant improvements in ankle plantarflexion strength and walking endurance. These findings support combining AIH with task-specific gait training in future trials.

papers.title: Regression-Based Balance Discordance Refines Prediction of Prospective Falls After Subacute Stroke: A Secondary Analysis of the LEAPS Trial
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo determine whether continuous, regression-based measures of balance discordance refine prediction of prospective, recurrent falls after subacute stroke relative to a previously published threshold-based classification in the same cohort, and to characterize how a purely data-driven, dimensionality-reduction-based composite expresses the same underlying measures. DesignSecondary, observational analysis of a randomized controlled trial. Recurrent falls were modeled using Andersen-Gill Cox proportional hazards regression with robust standard errors clustered by participant. SettingFive-site, National Institutes of Health/National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke funded multicenter trial (Locomotor Experience Applied Post-Stroke, LEAPS). Participants384 adults with subacute stroke (of 408 randomized in the parent trial) with valid baseline balance confidence, walking, and balance scores and at least one recorded follow-up interval (2,357 person-intervals, 179 fall events). Main Outcome MeasuresProspective, recurrent falls over 12 months, ascertained via self-report falls diary. Balance discordance was computed as the residual from regressing balance confidence on objective walking distance, Berg Balance Scale performance, or both jointly (multivariable discordance); threshold-based classification used established cut-points on the same measures and principal component analysis served as secondary comparators. ResultsSingle-variable discordance was associated with lower fall hazard (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.79, 95% CI 0.63-0.99, p = .037), and multivariable discordance was associated with higher fall hazard (HR = 1.27, 95% CI 1.03-1.58, p = .026). None of three threshold-based classification indicators reached significance. Multivariable discordance and a three-component principal-component composite showed comparable model fit (concordance 0.616 vs. 0.618) and were substantially correlated (R2 = .49). ConclusionsContinuous, regression-based balance discordance predicted prospective, recurrent falls where a previously published threshold-based classification did not. The divergent direction of single- and multivariable findings suggests overconfidence relative to combined objective function, rather than confidence broadly, may be the more specific marker of fall risk.

papers.title: The development and psychometric evaluation of the Post Activity Symptom Scale (PASS) for Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/ Chronic Fatigue Syndrome.
papers.abstract: PurposeTo develop and psychometrically evaluate a new scale measuring post-exertional malaise in people with myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME)/ chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS). MethodsA draft scale was co-produced with patient and clinician advisory groups. After extensive pilot testing, adults with ME/CFS completed the Post Activity Symptom Scale online and repeated it two weeks later to assess test-retest reliability and sensitivity to change. Rasch analysis assessed each domain for unidimensionality, targeting, internal reliability, item fit and local dependency. Then Rasch-transformed interval data and parametric statistics were used to assess criterion-related and discriminant validity (by comparison with measures of physical health and ME/CFS severity), test-retest reliability and minimal detectable difference. ResultsThe item regarding delay in PEM onset was an under-discriminating misfit anomaly which was inconsistent with the remaining PASS items. When this was removed, the PASS was a unidimensional, psychometrically robust scale. Criterion-related validity (r=0.58, p<0.001) was moderate and highly significant, discriminant validity (p<0.001) and test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.81) were excellent. The minimal detectable difference was 1.93/100. Participants found the PASS easy to complete, comprehensive and relevant. ConclusionThe Post Activity Symptom Scale is a valid, reliable, sensitive measure of people of PEM in ME/CFS

papers.title: Midlife mobility assessment from the pocket: agreement and consistency between smartphone placement configurations
papers.abstract: Subtle declines in mobility may emerge during midlife and can be detected using smartphone-based motion measures. Instrumented assessment of balance and functional tasks commonly uses lower-back placement, which requires device fixation and may limit convenient real-world monitoring. This study compared mobility outcomes obtained from a practical front-pocket/thigh placement with those from a standardized lower-back placement during static balance, sit-to-stand (STS), and Timed Up and Go (TUG) tests. Forty-six adults aged 40-64 years completed static balance, 30-second STS, and TUG assessments during simultaneous smartphone recording at the lower back and pocket/thigh. Outcomes included two- and three-dimensional sway, STS repetition count, average repetition duration, lower limb power, and maximal vertical velocity, as well as TUG total duration and peak yaw angular velocity during both turns. Associations, intraclass correlation coefficients, and Bland-Altman analyses were used to characterize the relationship and agreement between the two placements. Balance outcomes showed strong correlations between placements (rs=0.83-0.93), with moderate-to-excellent consistency for most conditions, although pocket/thigh sway values were systematically higher. TUG total duration showed strong correlation and good absolute agreement (rs=0.895; ICC=0.881), and turning velocity showed good consistency during the first and the second turns. STS repetition count and average repetition duration demonstrated strong correlations between placements (r=0.996 and 0.985, respectively), with excellent absolute agreement for repetition count and excellent consistency for average repetition duration (ICC=0.993 and 0.982, respectively). In contrast, STS power and maximal vertical velocity showed weaker correlations and consistency (r=0.709 and rs=0.382; ICC=0.600 and 0.417, respectively). Pocket/thigh smartphone placement supports practical mobility assessment across balance, STS and TUG. Although some movement-derived measures showed placement-dependent differences in absolute values, relative performance patterns were generally preserved across placements. These findings support the development of pocket-based smartphone assessment for simplified and potentially unsupervised mobility monitoring in midlife, while placement-sensitive outcomes require further validation against external reference measures. Author SummaryWearable technologies, including smartphones, offer promising ways to assess mobility during midlife, when subtle changes in physical performance may begin to emerge but go undetected by conventional clinical tests. However, most research using these technologies has been conducted under controlled conditions, with devices often attached to the lower back. Although this approach provides useful measurements, it requires fixation, making it less practical for everyday use. In this study, we examined whether smartphones carried in a front pocket could provide mobility measurements comparable to those obtained from the lower back. Forty-six middle-aged adults completed balance, chair-standing, and walking and turning tasks while smartphones recorded their movements at both locations. We found that measures of mobility, such as chair-standing repetitions and walking task completion time, were highly comparable between smartphone locations. Balance measurements, such as body sway while standing on one leg, showed similar patterns, although their absolute values differed. In contrast, measures of muscle power and maximum upward movement speed during chair-standing were more sensitive to smartphone placement. Our findings support the potential of pocket-based smartphone assessment as a practical approach to measuring mobility beginning in midlife, while further research is needed to establish its suitability for everyday use.

papers.title: Development and psychometric evaluation of the Severity of Myalgic Encephalomyelitis Scale (SoMES) and the Myalgic Encephalomyelitis Occupational Status Scale (MEOSS)
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo develop and psychometrically evaluate two new brief assessments measuring disease severity (the Severity of ME Scale, SoMES) and occupational status (the ME Occupational Status Scale, MEOSS) in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) MethodsDraft SoMES and MEOSS were co-produced from relevant literature and lived experience. An online survey completed by adults with ME/CFS and was repeated two weeks later to assess reliability. The SF-36 (physical function) assessed criterion-related validity (Spearmann correlations) and discriminant validity (Kruskal-Wallis tests). Weighted kappa co-efficients assessed test-retest reliability and measurement error calculated minimal detectable difference (MDD). Results995 adults with ME/CFS participated and 579 completed the retest survey. Construct validity was confirmed from feedback. Criterion related validity was moderate-good (SoMES r = 0.663, MEOSS r=0.472, both p<0.001). Discriminant validity was demonstrated by significant differences in SF36-PF scores in different levels of SoMES and MEOSS (p=0.003 - 0.0001). SoMES test-retest reliability was moderate (k =0.53, P<0.001) with a MDD of 1.6, and excellent for the MEOSS (k = 0.76 p<.001) and the MDD was 1.4 ConclusionsThe Severity of ME Scale (SoMES) and the ME Occupational Status Scale (MEOSS) are valid, reliable, sensitive assessments of ME/CFS severity and occupational status respectively.

papers.title: LOW-FREQUENCY DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION PROMOTES LONG-TERM OROFACIAL MOTOR RECOVERY AFTER TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY: A CASE STUDY
papers.abstract: Diffuse axonal injury (DAI), a subtype of traumatic brain injury (TBI), can disrupt corticobulbar pathways, leading to chronic deficits in speech and swallowing. We present a first-in-human case study demonstrating the long-term therapeutic potential of low-frequency continuous deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the motor thalamus to restore corticobulbar function in a patient with severe DAI and persistent dysarthria and dysphagia. The patient underwent bilateral motor thalamus DBS implantation one-year post-injury for treatment of post-traumatic action tremor, and stimulation was delivered chronically at 55 Hz over three years of follow-up. We assessed orofacial motor outcomes using kinematic analysis of facial movements, videofluoroscopic swallowing studies, and speech tasks to dissociate the immediate assistive effects of stimulation (DBS ON versus OFF) from its long-term therapeutic effects (DBS OFF over time). Continuous DBS led to progressive recovery of facial symmetry, resolution of laryngeal penetration, and marked improvements in respiratory and phonatory control and speech intelligibility. While improvements in gross orofacial motor function persisted in the absence of stimulation, fine articulatory control remained dependent on ongoing stimulation or adjunct speech therapy for optimal performance. Stimulation-induced improvements in cervical posture may also have contributed to enhanced biomechanics of swallowing and voice production. These findings provide early evidence that low-frequency motor thalamus DBS may promote therapeutic benefits and extend the window of functional recovery in chronic TBI patients.

papers.title: Smaller Cortical Responses to Balance Perturbations in Parkinson's Disease with Freezing of Gait
papers.abstract: Freezing of gait (FoG) is among the most disabling symptoms of Parkinsons disease (PD) and is associated with balance impairment and increased falls risk, yet remains challenging to understand due to its episodic and context-dependent nature. Altered supplementary motor area (SMA) function at rest and before self-initiated movements has been implicated in FoG; however, whether this extends to functionally relevant balance behavior is unknown. A loss of balance in response to support surface translations during standing elicits a perturbation-evoked N1 potential, an error assessment signal linked to SMA activity. We therefore predicted that people with FoG would have smaller and later N1 responses than people with PD without FoG and older adults. We recorded electroencephalography (EEG) during backward support-surface translations in 29 people with PD (71 {+/-} 7 years), including 13 people with a history of FoG (FoG+) and 16 people without FoG (FoG-), and 26 older adults (OA; 67 {+/-} 6 years). N1 amplitude and latency were quantified at a central midline electrode and defined as the largest negative peak 100-300 ms post-perturbation. N1 responses were similar between OA and FoG-({Delta} = 4.0 {micro}V and 2.8 ms, respectively). In contrast, FoG+ had smaller N1 amplitudes than FoG- ({Delta} = 18.1 {micro}V, p = 0.001) and OA ({Delta} = 14.1 {micro}V, p = 0.003), and both differences persisted after adjusting for age. FoG+ also had later N1 latencies than OA ({Delta} = 26.5 ms, p = 0.029), with a similar but non-significant difference versus FoG- ({Delta} = 23.6 ms, p = 0.091); after adjusting for age, these latency differences were not retained. These findings suggest that perturbation-evoked cortical activity is altered in FoG, potentially reflecting altered SMA function, and may provide a functionally relevant marker of FoG susceptibility.

papers.title: Effects of Weighted Seated Core Exercises on Immediate Postural Stability in Healthy Young Adults: An Exploratory Study
papers.abstract: ObjectivesThis exploratory study investigated whether low-load, seated core exercises could produce immediate improvements in standing balance among healthy young adults, aiming to provide a foundation for safe, early-stage rehabilitation protocols. MethodsTen healthy males performed seated core exercises consisted of alternating hip flexion 5 times per side while seated and maintaining bilateral shoulder flexion at 120{degrees} shoulder flexion under four load conditions: upper-limb weight only, a 400-g empty box, a 1-kg ball, and a 2-kg ball. Immediately following the exercise, participants performed a 10-s single-leg stance. Transversus abdominis (TrA) thickness was measured via wireless ultrasound at baseline, post-exercise, and during the stance. Center of pressure (CoP) sway was recorded concurrently to evaluate postural stability. ResultsLeft-side TrA thickness during stance increased significantly under the 1-kg and 2-kg load conditions compared to baseline (p 0.05). A moderate positive correlation ({rho} = 0.43, p = 0.002) was found between right-side TrA thickness and CoP sway velocity during the single-leg stance. ConclusionsLow-load, seated core exercises do not yield immediate enhancements in standing stability in healthy populations. The results suggest that increased TrA thickness during a balance task may correlate with heightened postural instability rather than improved balance control. Further research is needed to determine whether these findings translate to clinical populations with impaired physical fitness.

papers.title: Technology Demonstration of a Portable Sensorimotor Assessment System after Short-Duration Spaceflight
papers.abstract: Astronauts experience sensorimotor dysfunction due to microgravity-induced adaptations, leading to impaired posture, locomotion, and manual control. This manuscript details a portable sensorimotor assessment system, including an ankle proprioception test and visual-vestibular tests in a virtual reality headset, which was successfully deployed as a technology demonstration for one astronaut participant pre- and post-spaceflight. Post-flight testing occurred 1 and 3 days after return to Earth (R+1, R+3), with ankle proprioception also tested at R+0. Compared to pre-flight, left ankle proprioception was decreased at R+0 (two standard deviations below the mean of normative data) and returned to pre-flight levels by R+1. All visual-vestibular parameters showed decreased performance post-flight (below the 25th percentile of normative data) and little recovery by R+3. While future validation is required, these assessments appear sensitive to post-flight sensorimotor deconditioning. Furthermore, this technology demonstration highlights the logistical considerations and operational compatibility of the assessments post-flight.

papers.title: Therapeutic acute intermittent hypoxia alters supraspinal neural control of lower limb movement in multiple sclerosis
papers.abstract: Acute intermittent hypoxia (AIH) therapy is a promising neurorehabilitative intervention with well- documented improvement in motor function in people with spinal cord injury. Its effect on lower-limb motor control in multiple sclerosis (MS), where walking impairment is a leading source of disability, remain uncharacterized, and the supraspinal effects of AIH therapy are unknown. In a sham-controlled, double-blind crossover trial (NCT05164705), 23 adults with MS completed 5 sessions of AIH therapy and of sham therapy; magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed before and after each therapeutic intervention. At each timepoint, blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) functional MRI was collected during a repeated plantar- and dorsi-flexion task. Task-evoked activation was modeled at the group level and compared across timepoint and therapeutic arm. Activation changes differed for the left- and right-foot task. AIH augmented activation in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and cortical motor regions during left-foot movement with similar but sub-threshold patterns for the right foot. Right-foot movement additionally showed enhanced deactivation in prefrontal, parietal, and temporal cortices, although these effects were primarily in white matter voxels, limiting their interpretability. These findings suggest that changes in subcortical activation may contribute to motor function improvements following AIH therapy, implicating the basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical motor loop as a target of AIH-induced neuroplasticity. These results also indicate that AIH therapy modulates supraspinal motor circuitry, supporting further investigation of the cortical and subcortical effects of this emerging therapeutic treatment.

papers.title: Effectiveness of Plyometric Exercises Versus Flatfoot Corrective Exercises on Balance and Foot Posture in Obese Children with a Flexible Flatfoot: A Comparative Study
papers.abstract: Background and PurposeChildhood obesity often leads to flexible flatfoot, which negatively affects foot posture, balance, and physical function. While exercise is commonly used in clinical practice, there is limited comparative evidence on plyometric training versus traditional corrective exercises in this population. This study aimed to compare the effects of an 8-week plyometric exercise program versus flatfoot corrective exercises on balance and foot posture in obese children aged 7-11 years with flexible flatfoot. MethodsA parallel, non-randomized comparative study was conducted with 120 children recruited from schools in Bengaluru. Participants were allocated to either Group A (plyometric exercises, n = 60) or Group B (flatfoot corrective exercises, n = 60). Both groups trained for 8 weeks (two 40-minute sessions weekly). Foot posture was assessed using the Foot Posture Index-6 (FPI-6), and static balance was measured as center-of-pressure path length using the BTrackS Balance Tracking System before and after the intervention. ResultsBoth groups demonstrated statistically significant within-group improvements in foot posture and balance after 8 weeks (p < 0.001). However, the plyometric group achieved slightly better improvements in foot posture (statistically significant for the left foot, p = 0.028) and markedly greater gains in balance (median path length: 30.39 cm vs. 37.45 cm, p< 0.001) compared to the corrective exercise group. ConclusionsBoth exercise approaches are beneficial for obese children with flexible flatfoot. Plyometric training provides additional advantages in improving dynamic balance and neuromuscular control, supporting its inclusion in pediatric physiotherapy programs.

papers.title: A Retrospective Real-World Assessment of Motor Status After Stroke Using a Home-Based Brain-Computer Interface
papers.abstract: BackgroundUpper extremity impairment persists in many stroke survivors, and few treatments are effective for severe chronic deficits. Brain-computer interface (BCI) therapy, which pairs decoded motor-intention-associated electrophysiology with sensory feedback, has improved upper extremity impairment in randomized trials, including in patients with severe paresis. Whether these benefits translate to routine care has rarely been evaluated. This study examined upper extremity motor recovery through 1 year among patients prescribed at-home BCI therapy in clinical practice. MethodsThis retrospective observational study included adults who were prescribed the IpsiHand System, an electroencephalography-based BCI, through a commercial US home therapy program, had a baseline Upper Extremity Fugl-Meyer (UEFM) assessment, and averaged >1 session per week through their last assessment. Occupational therapists administered the UEFM by video every 4 weeks. The primary outcome was UEFM change from baseline to week 12. A mixed model for repeated measures estimated change through week 52, with multiple imputation sensitivity analyses for missing data. ResultsOf 452 patients included in analyses (mean time since stroke, 5.4{+/-}5.4 years), mean baseline UEFM was 20.1{+/-}14.6, with 333 patients (73.7%) having severe motor impairment (UEFM 0-28). At week 12, mean UEFM change was 4.3 points (95% CI, 3.7-4.9; P<0.001), and 31.7% achieved the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) of 5.25 points. Mean change reached the MCID at week 16 (5.6, 95% CI [4.8, 6.4]). Model-estimated change in UEFM continued to improve through 1 year, being 6.1 (95% CI, 5.5-6.8) at week 24 and 8.1 (95% CI, 6.8-9.4) at week 52. ConclusionsAmong regular users of at-home BCI therapy in routine care, most of whom had severe chronic impairment, UEFM scores improved by 12 weeks, reached MCID by 16 weeks, and continued to increase through 1 year. At-home BCI therapy merits evaluation in randomized trials with follow-up beyond 12 weeks.

papers.title: Predicting Robot-Based Tracking Performance After Stroke Using Lesion Features and Clinical Assessments: A Pilot Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundFollowing stroke, motor and cognitive impairments often limit functional independence. Personalized rehabilitation requires comprehensive clinical assessments, which are costly and time-consuming. Imaging scans are routinely collected, but their predictive value in determining post-stroke function remains unclear. ObjectivesTo determine the ability of clinical assessments, lesion features with medical chart information, and a combined clinical and biomedical model to predict kinematic outcomes from a robot-based tracking task in chronic stroke individuals. MethodsEighteen participants (70{+/-}6 years) completed a robot-based tracking task and a battery of motor and cognitive assessments. Three elastic net regression models were developed: 1) clinical assessments only; 2) lesion metrics and chart information only; and 3) a combined model. Models were evaluated using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, bootstrapping, and permutation testing with false discovery rate correction. Robot-based outcomes included tracking error, normalized distance, velocity error response, and delay. ResultsThe clinical assessment model significantly predicted tracking error (R{superscript 2}=0.45), delay (R{superscript 2}=0.22), velocity error response (R{superscript 2}=0.18), and normalized distance (R{superscript 2}=0.12). The combined model significantly predicted tracking error (R{superscript 2}=0.37), delay (R{superscript 2}=0.19), and velocity error response (R{superscript 2}=0.11). The imaging model did not significantly predict any outcome. Box and Blocks Test and Color Trails 1 were stable features. The right dorsal attention network was a stable predictor in several combined models. ConclusionClinical assessments outperformed lesion features in predicting tracking performance after chronic stroke. Attention- and motor-related measures were the strongest predictors, highlighting the importance of cognitive-motor interactions in function. A larger sample and more granular lesion features may improve prediction from imaging biomarkers.

papers.title: Remote Ischemic Conditioning Modulates Spinal Reflex Excitability in Healthy Young Adults: A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
papers.abstract: BackgroundRemote ischemic conditioning (RIC), involving transient and sublethal bouts of ischemia and reperfusion, promotes neuroplasticity and motor learning. Although early clinical studies suggest supraspinal and muscular mechanisms underlying RIC, its influence on spinal reflex excitability - a key substrate for motor learning - remains poorly understood. Balance training alone is known to modulate spinal excitability, but whether RIC can enhance this training-induced adaptation has not been tested. ObjectiveThis prospective single-blind, pilot randomized controlled trial (RCT) explored the preliminary effects of pairing RIC with balance training on spinal reflex excitability and balance performance in healthy young adults and generated estimates of variability to inform a future definitive randomized trial. MethodsTwenty-six participants aged between 18-40 years were randomized to RIC or sham groups at university-based research setting between March and August 2025. The intervention included five cycles of 5-minute cuff inflation (RIC: 200 mmHg; sham: 25 mmHg) and 5-minute deflation on the dominant thigh, followed by balance training on a stability platform (15 trials/day) for five consecutive days. Pre- and post-intervention assessments included Hoffmanns reflex (H-reflex) parameters--Hmax (peak H-reflex amplitude reflecting motor neuron recruitment via Ia afferent input), H/M ratio (Hmax normalized to maximal M-wave amplitude), Hslp/Mslp ratio (relative slope of the H-reflex and M-wave recruitment curves), and H-reflex threshold (minimum stimulus intensity eliciting a response)--used to index spinal motor neuron pool excitability, as well as balance performance, quantified as center time (the duration participants maintained a stability platform within a set horizontal threshold). Independent sample and Mann-Whitney U tests analyzed the differences in the change scores (RIC vs Sham) for H-reflex and balance outcomes respectively. ResultsThe RIC group showed directionally greater reduction in the Hslp/ Mslp ratio (p = 0.02) and greater improvement in balance performance (p = 0.02) compared to sham group. No significant between-group differences were observed for Hmax, H/M ratio, or H-reflex threshold; however, the direction of changes in Hmax was consistent with reduced spinal reflex excitability following RIC. These findings potentially suggest that RIC could augment the neuroplastic adaptations typically induced by balance training. ConclusionThis pilot study provides preliminary evidence that RIC paired with balance training may influence selected spinal neurophysiological responses and improve balance performance in healthy adults. The potential convergence of neurophysiological and behavioral adaptations observed in this pilot study may suggest a role for RIC as a physiological primer for sensorimotor learning. Moreover, these findings establish a foundation for future large-scale trials incorporating cortical and presynaptic inhibitory measures to elucidate mechanisms and clinical applicability in neurological populations.

papers.title: Evaluating ChatGPTs Responses to Chiropractic Patient Questions: A Comparative Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundLarge language models (LLMs) are used at an increased frequency by patients to answer health related questions. Prior studies have evaluated LLMs and their performance with musculoskeletal (MSK) and spine domains, but have not been used to evaluate chiropractic-relevant content. ObjectiveTo evaluate ChatGPT responses to commonly asked chiropractic patient questions for concordance with chiropractic clinical practice guidelines. MethodsThirty questions addressing low back pain, neck pain, and chronic musculoskeletal pain were developed based on current U.S. chiropractic clinical practice guidelines (CPGs). ChatGPT (GPT-5.2) generated responses in isolated sessions. Responses were assessed for readability using established indices, then five licensed chiropractors independently rated each response using a 5-point Likert scale across four domains: relevance, clarity, completeness, and accuracy. Inter-rater reliability was evaluated using Krippendorffs alpha (ordinal). ResultsReadability measures demonstrated that ChatGPT responses were written at approximately a college-level reading grade. Expert ratings across all domain means (standard deviation) were predominately clustered at the upper end of rating scale (1-5): Relevance 4.72 {+/-} 0.56; Clarity 4.76 {+/-} 0.50; Completeness 4.23 {+/-} 0.81; Accuracy 4.00 {+/-} 1.02. The Krippendorffs alpha (ordinal) ranged from -0.023-0.214 across the domains, all reflective of poor inter-rater reliability. ConclusionChatGPT responses were broadly consistent with chiropractic CPGs, though readability levels exceeded recommended patient education standards. While the expert panel frequently assigned similar scores, minor scoring differences and restricted score distributions produced low chance-corrected reliability. These findings suggest that ChatGPT can produce guideline concordant responses but readability and interpretive variability should be considered when integrating LLM generated information into patient education.
